This transfers vibration into the operator’s hands, wrists, arms, and joints, creating discomfort, fatigue, and possible injury. Furthermore, stronger coupling generally requires greater hand pressure, which increases the vibration experienced by the operator.

An air-extraction mechanism, such as a vacuum pump, is also coupled to the first side and is in fluid communication with a chamber located on a second side of the base. 12	
13	Unlike conventional vacuum grippers or suction cups, the rigid perimeter is not intended to form a complete airtight seal and does not rely on flexible rubber or foam. Instead, it restricts airflow into the chamber while maintaining rigid contact with the tile. The air-extraction mechanism continuously removes air entering beneath the rigid perimeter, maintaining the chamber at a lower pressure than the surrounding atmosphere. The resulting pressure differential holds the device firmly against the tile without requiring the operator to press downward.

At the same time, the low-friction perimeter allows the device to slide freely across different areas of the tile while the vacuum continuously maintains contact.
16	
17	The device may include one or more handles used primarily for guiding the machine rather than pressing it against the surface. In another embodiment, a rope, wire, cable, or similar flexible pulling element is connected to the device. Pulling the flexible element moves the device across the tile, while the pressure differential independently supplies the force holding the device against the surface. This provides decoupled control in which the operator controls position using minimal pulling force while the vacuum maintains consistent coupling and vibration transfer. The invention therefore maximizes vibration delivered to the tile while minimizing vibration, pressure, fatigue, and joint stress experienced by the operator.

This is the ONLY authority for what the invention includes. Everything you claim must be supported here or in later messages from the user.

The present invention relates to a vibration device for setting tiles and other covering materials into thinset, mortar, adhesive, or similar bonding material. Conventional tile vibrators generally include a vibrating motor connected to a handle and either a smooth sliding base or a flexible suction cup. The vibration is intended to remove trapped air, distribute the bonding material, improve surface contact, and strengthen the bond between the tile and the underlying substrate.

Existing systems have two main disadvantages. First, vibration from the motor is not efficiently coupled to the tile. A smooth sliding base must be pressed firmly against the tile by the operator, and even then a thin layer of air between the base and the tile may dampen vibration transfer. A suction-cup system creates a stronger connection, but the flexible rubber or foam forming the suction cup absorbs and dampens part of the vibration. A conventional suction cup also attaches the machine at one fixed location, preventing it from sliding across the tile and causing vibration intensity to decrease at areas farther from the attachment point.

Second, existing systems require the operator to continuously apply substantial downward pressure to maintain contact with the tile. This transfers vibration into the operator’s hands, wrists, arms, and joints, creating discomfort, fatigue, and possible injury. Shock absorbers and vibration-damping handles may reduce some vibration reaching the operator, but they also absorb mechanical energy that could otherwise be transferred to the tile. Furthermore, stronger coupling generally requires greater hand pressure, which increases the vibration experienced by the operator.

The invention addresses these problems by providing a vibration motor coupled to a first side of a rigid base. An air-extraction mechanism, such as a vacuum pump, is also coupled to the first side and is in fluid communication with a chamber located on a second side of the base. The perimeter of the second side is formed as a rigid loop or skirt made from a low-friction material such as plastic, metal, PTFE, or a combination of rigid materials.

Unlike conventional vacuum grippers or suction cups, the rigid perimeter is not intended to form a complete airtight seal and does not rely on flexible rubber or foam. Instead, it restricts airflow into the chamber while maintaining rigid contact with the tile. The air-extraction mechanism continuously removes air entering beneath the rigid perimeter, maintaining the chamber at a lower pressure than the surrounding atmosphere. The resulting pressure differential holds the device firmly against the tile without requiring the operator to press downward.

Because the vibration motor is connected to the tile through rigid components, vibration energy is transferred with substantially less damping than through a flexible suction cup. At the same time, the low-friction perimeter allows the device to slide freely across different areas of the tile while the vacuum continuously maintains contact.

The device may include one or more handles used primarily for guiding the machine rather than pressing it against the surface. In another embodiment, a rope, wire, cable, or similar flexible pulling element is connected to the device. Pulling the flexible element moves the device across the tile, while the pressure differential independently supplies the force holding the device against the surface. This provides decoupled control in which the operator controls position using minimal pulling force while the vacuum maintains consistent coupling and vibration transfer. The invention therefore maximizes vibration delivered to the tile while minimizing vibration, pressure, fatigue, and joint stress experienced by the operator.

Here is my invention.

The present invention relates to a vibration device for setting tiles and other covering materials into thinset, mortar, adhesive, or similar bonding material. Conventional tile vibrators generally include a vibrating motor connected to a handle and either a smooth sliding base or a flexible suction cup. The vibration is intended to remove trapped air, distribute the bonding material, improve surface contact, and strengthen the bond between the tile and the underlying substrate.

Existing systems have two main disadvantages. First, vibration from the motor is not efficiently coupled to the tile. A smooth sliding base must be pressed firmly against the tile by the operator, and even then a thin layer of air between the base and the tile may dampen vibration transfer. A suction-cup system creates a stronger connection, but the flexible rubber or foam forming the suction cup absorbs and dampens part of the vibration. A conventional suction cup also attaches the machine at one fixed location, preventing it from sliding across the tile and causing vibration intensity to decrease at areas farther from the attachment point.

Second, existing systems require the operator to continuously apply substantial downward pressure to maintain contact with the tile. This transfers vibration into the operator’s hands, wrists, arms, and joints, creating discomfort, fatigue, and possible injury. Shock absorbers and vibration-damping handles may reduce some vibration reaching the operator, but they also absorb mechanical energy that could otherwise be transferred to the tile. Furthermore, stronger coupling generally requires greater hand pressure, which increases the vibration experienced by the operator.

The invention addresses these problems by providing a vibration motor coupled to a first side of a rigid base. An air-extraction mechanism, such as a vacuum pump, is also coupled to the first side and is in fluid communication with a chamber located on a second side of the base. The perimeter of the second side is formed as a rigid loop or skirt made from a low-friction material such as plastic, metal, PTFE, or a combination of rigid materials.

Unlike conventional vacuum grippers or suction cups, the rigid perimeter is not intended to form a complete airtight seal and does not rely on flexible rubber or foam. Instead, it restricts airflow into the chamber while maintaining rigid contact with the tile. The air-extraction mechanism continuously removes air entering beneath the rigid perimeter, maintaining the chamber at a lower pressure than the surrounding atmosphere. The resulting pressure differential holds the device firmly against the tile without requiring the operator to press downward.

Because the vibration motor is connected to the tile through rigid components, vibration energy is transferred with substantially less damping than through a flexible suction cup. At the same time, the low-friction perimeter allows the device to slide freely across different areas of the tile while the vacuum continuously maintains contact.

The device may include one or more handles used primarily for guiding the machine rather than pressing it against the surface. In another embodiment, a rope, wire, cable, or similar flexible pulling element is connected to the device. Pulling the flexible element moves the device across the tile, while the pressure differential independently supplies the force holding the device against the surface. This provides decoupled control in which the operator controls position using minimal pulling force while the vacuum maintains consistent coupling and vibration transfer. The invention therefore maximizes vibration delivered to the tile while minimizing vibration, pressure, fatigue, and joint stress experienced by the operator.

Mechanical vibration applied to the exposed face of the covering element after it is laid drives the trapped air out, spreads the bonding material into a more uniform layer, increases the area over which the bonding material actually touches the covering element, and thereby improves the strength of the completed bond. Hand-guided vibration devices are used for this purpose.

3	Such devices generally comprise a vibration motor carried on a handle together with one of two arrangements for putting the vibration into the covering element: a smooth sliding base that the operator presses down onto the exposed face, or a flexible suction cup that grips the exposed face at one place.

1	In the following description, the same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout the drawings. The embodiments described are examples and do not limit the scope of what is claimed.
2	
3	Overview
4	
5	FIG. 1 and FIG. 2 show a vibration device 10 in use, and FIG. 4 shows the bedded layers beneath it in enlarged detail. A covering element 36, which may be a tile or other covering material, has been laid onto a bed of bonding material 40 spread over a substrate 42, as seen in FIG. 4. The bonding material 40 may be thinset, mortar, tile adhesive or any similar bonding material that is plastic when the covering element 36 is laid and hardens afterwards. The substrate 42 is the surface being covered. The covering element 36 presents an exposed face 38 facing away from the bonding material 40. The vibration device 10 rests on the exposed face 38 and delivers vibration into the covering element 36, which drives trapped air out of the bonding material 40, distributes the bonding material 40 more evenly beneath the covering element 36, increases the proportion of the underside of the covering element 36 that is wetted by the bonding material 40, and improves the contact between the covering element 36 and the bonding material 40.
6	
7	The vibration device 10 comprises a base 12, a vibration motor 18, an air-extraction mechanism 20 and a perimeter member 24. The base 12 is rigid and has a first side 14 facing away from the covering element 36 and a second side 16 facing the covering element 36. The vibration motor 18 is coupled to the first side 14. The air-extraction mechanism 20 is also coupled to the first side 14 and is in fluid communication with a chamber 22 located on the second side 16. The perimeter member 24 extends from the second side 16 around the chamber 22 and terminates in a bearing face 26 that contacts the exposed face 38.
8	
9	The base
10	
11	The base 12 is rigid: under the alternating force produced by the vibration motor 18 and under the pressure differential described below, the base 12 does not deflect enough to absorb an appreciable fraction of the vibration energy, and it transmits that energy to the perimeter member 24 substantially undiminished.
12	
13	The second side 16 of the base 12 forms the upper boundary of the chamber 22, and the chamber 22 is in fluid communication with the air-extraction mechanism 20.
14	
15	The vibration motor
16	
17	The vibration motor 18 is coupled to the first side 14 of the base 12, with no resilient mount, rubber bush or foam pad interposed between the vibration motor 18 and the base 12. That direct coupling is intentional. A resilient motor mount would isolate the base 12 from the vibration motor 18, which is the opposite of what is wanted: the entire object of the device is to put vibration into the covering element 36, and any compliant member anywhere between the vibration motor 18 and the exposed face 38 removes energy from that transfer.
18	
19	The vibration motor 18 may be of any type that produces mechanical vibration in the base 12. What matters to the arrangement described here is not the mechanism by which the vibration is generated but the path by which it leaves the vibration device 10, which is dealt with below.
20	
21	The air-extraction mechanism
22	
23	The air-extraction mechanism 20 is coupled to the first side 14 of the base 12 and withdraws air from the chamber 22. In the embodiment shown, the air-extraction mechanism 20 is a vacuum pump carried on the base 12.
24	
25	The air-extraction mechanism 20 runs continuously while the vibration device 10 is in use. It is not run to establish a vacuum and then stopped: the chamber 22 is never sealed, so the pressure differential exists only while the air-extraction mechanism 20 withdraws air from the chamber 22.
26	
27	The perimeter member and the chamber
28	
29	A perimeter member 24 stands proud of the second side 16 and surrounds the chamber 22: a rigid loop, or skirt, that runs round the second side 16 near its perimeter. In the embodiment of FIG. 3 the perimeter member 24 is a closed loop running around the second side 16 at its perimeter. The perimeter member 24, the second side 16 of the base 12 and, in use, the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36 together bound the chamber 22. The chamber 22 is a single space bounded by one perimeter member 24, as shown in FIG. 2. The joint between the perimeter member 24 and the base 12 is rigid and carries vibration across itself without loss.
30	
31	The perimeter member 24 terminates, at its end remote from the base 12, in a bearing face 26 that contacts the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. The bearing face 26 is a low-friction material. Suitable materials are plastic, metal, polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE), and combinations of rigid materials. The perimeter member 24 is made of a low-friction rigid material, and the bearing face 26 is the end face of that member.
32	
33	The perimeter member 24 is not a seal. It is free of rubber, elastomer and foam. This distinguishes it from a suction cup and from a compliant sealing skirt, and the difference is functional rather than nominal. A suction cup works by conforming to the surface, closing the enclosed space against the atmosphere, and holding the reduced pressure inside; conforming requires compliance, and compliance in the load path damps vibration. The perimeter member 24 is instead hard and dimensionally stable, and it makes rigid contact with the exposed face 38.
34	
35	Because the perimeter member 24 is rigid and the exposed face 38 is neither perfectly flat nor perfectly clean, in that it carries dust, grains of bonding material 40 and its own surface texture, and the covering element 36 itself may be slightly bowed, a clearance 34 remains between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38 along at least part of the perimeter member 24, as shown enlarged in FIG. 4, which is an enlarged fragmentary detail of the lower end of a perimeter member 24 of the general kind shown in FIG. 2, taken at a place along the loop where the clearance 34 is present. The clearance 34 is far too small to be drawn to scale, and so are the departures from flatness of the exposed face 38 that give rise to it. FIG. 2 accordingly shows the perimeter member 24 resting on the covering element 36 without any gap, at the scale of that view, and the clearance 34 appears only in the enlarged detail of FIG. 4, where it is drawn many times its true height. The enlarged detail of FIG. 4 also shows the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, and the covering element 36 bedded in the bonding material 40 that has been spread over the substrate 42. Ambient air passes through the clearance 34 into the chamber 22 continuously while the vibration device 10 is in use. The clearance 34 is not a defect to be eliminated. It is the condition the vibration device 10 is designed to work in: the perimeter member 24 restricts the flow of ambient air into the chamber 22, and does so by presenting a long, narrow, high-resistance path around the whole loop, without closing that path.
36	
37	The pressure differential that holds the device down
38	
39	The air-extraction mechanism 20 withdraws air from the chamber 22 at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber 22 below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter through the clearance 34, for as long as the air-extraction mechanism 20 runs.
40	
41	The difference between atmospheric pressure and the pressure in the chamber 22, acting over the plan area of the chamber 22, produces a holding force that presses the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36. The holding force is sufficient to hold the vibration device 10 against the exposed face 38 without any downward force being applied by an operator. In use the operator's hands carry no part of the contact load.
42	
43	A property of this arrangement should be noted, because it is what the arrangement is for.
44	
45	The vibration device 10 can be translated across the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is being maintained. The pressure differential is maintained continuously throughout the translating, so that the vibration device 10 is held against the covering element 36 and slid over the exposed face 38 at the same time; holding and sliding are simultaneous, not alternatives. The bearing face 26, being of a low-friction material, is slidable over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is maintained, and slides under the holding force with a modest in-plane resistance, and the air-extraction mechanism 20 continues to run and continues to hold the vibration device 10 down throughout the movement. No mode has to be switched, no air cushion has to be raised under the device, and no grip has to be released and re-established. Vibration can therefore be delivered to successive areas of the covering element 36 at full amplitude, instead of falling away with distance from a single fixed attachment point.
46	
47	The vibration transmission path
48	
49	The vibration transmission path runs as follows. Vibration produced by the vibration motor 18 passes into the base 12 at the first side 14, along the base 12, into the perimeter member 24 through the rigid joint at the second side 16, along the perimeter member 24, and out through the bearing face 26 into the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. Every member in that path, namely the base 12 and the perimeter member 24 terminating in the bearing face 26, is rigid, and no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount is interposed anywhere along it. The vibration therefore reaches the covering element 36 with substantially less damping than it would in an arrangement in which a flexible suction cup, a resilient motor mount or a vibration-damping handle lies in the path.
50	
51	The holding force from the pressure differential also acts to keep the bearing face 26 in contact with the exposed face 38 throughout each vibration cycle. Contact is maintained by a force that does not vary with what the operator is doing, which is what makes the transfer consistent across the working area and from one operator to the next.
52	
53	The clearance 34 does not stand between the bearing face 26 and the covering element 36 in the way that a film of air stands between a pressed-on sliding base and the covering element beneath it. A sliding base of that kind is separated from the covering element over its whole area, so that everything crossing the interface must cross the film, and the film, being compressible, both stores and dissipates part of what crosses it. Here the bearing face 26 is loaded onto the exposed face 38 by the holding force and makes hard, direct contact with it over the remainder of the loop, and it is that contact, not the clearance 34, that carries the vibration. The clearance 34 is a leakage path in parallel with the contact rather than a compliant layer in series with it: air passes along it, edgewise, into the chamber 22, and the vibration passes across the contact beside it. Nothing compressible is interposed in the load path, and the holding force presses the contact together rather than holding the two faces apart.
54	
55	The force balance on the vibration device 10 in use is as follows. The weight of the vibration device 10 and the holding force act downward on the covering element 36; the reaction of the exposed face 38 acts upward; the frictional resistance of the bearing face 26 acts in the plane of the exposed face 38 and opposes translation; and the only force the operator supplies is an in-plane force sufficient to overcome that frictional resistance and to steer. Because the operator applies no downward force, there is no loaded path from the vibrating device into the operator's hands, wrists, arms and joints. The vibration reaching the operator is reduced not by absorbing it in a damper, which would take the same energy away from the covering element 36, but by removing the operator from the load path altogether. The usual trade-off, in which stronger coupling to the covering element 36 is bought with greater hand pressure and therefore with greater vibration exposure, does not arise here: the coupling is set by the air-extraction mechanism 20 and the operator's grip has nothing to do with it.
56	
57	Handles
58	
59	One or more handles 44 may be coupled to the base 12. The handle 44 is arranged to guide the vibration device 10 over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential holds the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36. It is not used to press the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36, and it need not be dimensioned or damped as though it were, because the contact load is supplied by the pressure differential.
60	
61	Embodiment with a flexible pulling element
62	
63	FIG. 5 shows a second embodiment. A flexible pulling element 46 is connected to the vibration device 10. The flexible pulling element 46 is a rope, wire, cable or similar flexible pulling element. The vibration device 10 is translatable over the exposed face 38 by tension applied to the flexible pulling element 46 while the pressure differential is maintained: the operator applies that tension and the vibration device 10 slides on the bearing face 26 in the direction of the applied tension.
64	
65	This embodiment gives decoupled control. The flexible pulling element 46 can transmit force only along its own length and, being flexible, cannot transmit compression at all. It therefore cannot press the vibration device 10 down against the covering element 36, whatever the operator does with it. The flexible pulling element 46 is thus incapable of transmitting compression to the vibration device 10, and moves it across the exposed face 38 when tension is applied. The force holding the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 is supplied independently, and continuously, by the pressure differential across the base 12. Position is thus controlled by one agency and contact by another: the operator sets where the vibration device 10 is with a small pulling force, while the quality of the vibration coupling is set by the air-extraction mechanism 20 and does not vary with how, how hard, or from what angle the operator pulls.
66	
67	Method of use
68	
69	A method of bedding a covering element 36 into bonding material 40 using the vibration device 10 is carried out as follows. The method begins with placing the vibration device 10 on the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, whereby the bearing face 26 of the perimeter member 24 is brought into contact with the exposed face 38 so that the chamber 22 is bounded by the second side 16, the perimeter member 24 and the exposed face 38, with the clearance 34 remaining, along at least part of the perimeter member 24, between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38. It continues with operating the air-extraction mechanism 20 to withdraw air from the chamber 22 at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber 22 below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter the chamber 22 through the clearance 34, the resulting pressure differential holding the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 without downward force applied by an operator. It continues with operating the vibration motor 18 and transmitting vibration from the vibration motor 18 to the covering element 36 through the base 12, the perimeter member 24 and the bearing face 26. It continues with translating the vibration device 10 across the exposed face 38, while the pressure differential is maintained, by sliding the bearing face 26 over the exposed face 38, so that vibration is delivered to successive areas of the covering element 36. The translating may be done by applying tension to the flexible pulling element 46, or by guiding the vibration device 10 with the handle 44.

The bearing face 26, being of a low-friction material, is slidable over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is maintained, and slides under the holding force with a modest in-plane resistance, and the air-extraction mechanism 20 continues to run and continues to hold the vibration device 10 down throughout the movement. No mode has to be switched, no air cushion has to be raised under the device, and no grip has to be released and re-established. Vibration can therefore be delivered to successive areas of the covering element 36 at full amplitude, instead of falling away with distance from a single fixed attachment point.

The vibration transmission path

The vibration transmission path runs as follows. Vibration produced by the vibration motor 18 passes into the base 12 at the first side 14, along the base 12, into the perimeter member 24 through the rigid joint at the second side 16, along the perimeter member 24, and out through the bearing face 26 into the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. Every member in that path, namely the base 12 and the perimeter member 24 terminating in the bearing face 26, is rigid, and no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount is interposed anywhere along it. The vibration therefore reaches the covering element 36 with substantially less damping than it would in an arrangement in which a flexible suction cup, a resilient motor mount or a vibration-damping handle lies in the path.

The holding force from the pressure differential also acts to keep the bearing face 26 in contact with the exposed face 38 throughout each vibration cycle. Contact is maintained by a force that does not vary with what the operator is doing, which is what makes the transfer consistent across the working area and from one operator to the next.

The clearance 34 does not stand between the bearing face 26 and the covering element 36 in the way that a film of air stands between a pressed-on sliding base and the covering element beneath it. A sliding base of that kind is separated from the covering element over its whole area, so that everything crossing the interface must cross the film, and the film, being compressible, both stores and dissipates part of what crosses it. Here the bearing face 26 is loaded onto the exposed face 38 by the holding force and makes hard, direct contact with it over the remainder of the loop, and it is that contact, not the clearance 34, that carries the vibration. The clearance 34 is a leakage path in parallel with the contact rather than a compliant layer in series with it: air passes along it, edgewise, into the chamber 22, and the vibration passes across the contact beside it. Nothing compressible is interposed in the load path, and the holding force presses the contact together rather than holding the two faces apart.

The force balance on the vibration device 10 in use is as follows. The weight of the vibration device 10 and the holding force act downward on the covering element 36; the reaction of the exposed face 38 acts upward; the frictional resistance of the bearing face 26 acts in the plane of the exposed face 38 and opposes translation; and the only force the operator supplies is an in-plane force sufficient to overcome that frictional resistance and to steer. Because the operator applies no downward force, there is no loaded path from the vibrating device into the operator's hands, wrists, arms and joints. The vibration reaching the operator is reduced not by absorbing it in a damper, which would take the same energy away from the covering element 36, but by removing the operator from the load path altogether. The usual trade-off, in which stronger coupling to the covering element 36 is bought with greater hand pressure and therefore with greater vibration exposure, does not arise here: the coupling is set by the air-extraction mechanism 20 and the operator's grip has nothing to do with it.

Handles

One or more handles 44 may be coupled to the base 12. The handle 44 is arranged to guide the vibration device 10 over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential holds the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36. It is not used to press the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36, and it need not be dimensioned or damped as though it were, because the contact load is supplied by the pressure differential.

Embodiment with a flexible pulling element

FIG. 5 shows a second embodiment. A flexible pulling element 46 is connected to the vibration device 10. The flexible pulling element 46 is a rope, wire, cable or similar flexible pulling element. The vibration device 10 is translatable over the exposed face 38 by tension applied to the flexible pulling element 46 while the pressure differential is maintained: the operator applies that tension and the vibration device 10 slides on the bearing face 26 in the direction of the applied tension.

This embodiment gives decoupled control. The flexible pulling element 46 can transmit force only along its own length and, being flexible, cannot transmit compression at all. It therefore cannot press the vibration device 10 down against the covering element 36, whatever the operator does with it. The flexible pulling element 46 is thus incapable of transmitting compression to the vibration device 10, and moves it across the exposed face 38 when tension is applied. The force holding the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 is supplied independently, and continuously, by the pressure differential across the base 12. Position is thus controlled by one agency and contact by another: the operator sets where the vibration device 10 is with a small pulling force, while the quality of the vibration coupling is set by the air-extraction mechanism 20 and does not vary with how, how hard, or from what angle the operator pulls.

Method of use

A method of bedding a covering element 36 into bonding material 40 using the vibration device 10 is carried out as follows. The method begins with placing the vibration device 10 on the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, whereby the bearing face 26 of the perimeter member 24 is brought into contact with the exposed face 38 so that the chamber 22 is bounded by the second side 16, the perimeter member 24 and the exposed face 38, with the clearance 34 remaining, along at least part of the perimeter member 24, between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38. It continues with operating the air-extraction mechanism 20 to withdraw air from the chamber 22 at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber 22 below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter the chamber 22 through the clearance 34, the resulting pressure differential holding the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 without downward force applied by an operator. It continues with operating the vibration motor 18 and transmitting vibration from the vibration motor 18 to the covering element 36 through the base 12, the perimeter member 24 and the bearing face 26. It continues with translating the vibration device 10 across the exposed face 38, while the pressure differential is maintained, by sliding the bearing face 26 over the exposed face 38, so that vibration is delivered to successive areas of the covering element 36. The translating may be done by applying tension to the flexible pulling element 46, or by guiding the vibration device 10 with the handle 44.

content.text: I've read the disclosure, the full conversation, all nine draft sections, the numeral table, and all five figure briefs, and traced every claim limitation, numbered part, and figure structure against the inventor's text.

input.summary: Ledger result: the invention's spine is faithfully traced. Every element of claim 1 (rigid base with first/second sides, motor on the first side, air-extraction mechanism on the first side in fluid communication with a second-side chamber, rigid low-friction perimeter loop that is not a seal, continuous ingress with sub-atmospheric chamber, operator-free holding force, all-rigid transmission path, sliding while held), the dependent ladder (closed loop at the perimeter, plastic/metal/PTFE, free of rubber/elastomer/foam, vacuum pump, continuous extraction, handle for guiding, rope/wire/cable pulling element with decoupled control), the system claim, and the method claim all map to exact affirmative passages in the disclosure (repeated verbatim in the single substantive USER turn). Every later USER turn is procedural or corrective and supplies no new inventor support; the last two turns expressly disclaim being disclosure. Title, cross-reference, field, background, summary, abstract and the 16-entry numeral table are clean, no numeral is used twice, every numeral in the text is tabled and appears on at least one sheet, and no drafting note, placeholder, bracketed request or open question survives anywhere in draft/ or figures/. Seventeen defects remain: six passages of untraced technical substance in the detailed description (the physical cause of the clearance, the high-resistance-path mechanism, the bonding-material cure property, the "air cushion"/"modest resistance"/"full amplitude" characterizations, operator-to-operator consistency, and the parallel/series air-film model), one untraced claim limitation carried in claim 10 and the description ("incapable of transmitting compression"), untraced figure layout and attachment positions in FIG. 1 and FIG. 5, and internal contradictions: FIG. 2 and FIG. 3 affirmatively negate any passage through the base yet the claims require fluid communication across it; FIG. 2/FIG. 3 place the loop inboard while claim 2 and the description put it at the perimeter of the second side; FIG. 1 shows the device resting on the tile with the perimeter member absent; and numeral 36 means one covering element in FIG. 2/FIG. 4 but a multi-tile floor in FIG. 5, labelled on a tile the device is not on. Not filing-ready as it stands; each finding below has a bounded, disclosure-grounded fix.

findings.title: Physical cause of the clearance (surface texture, dust, grains, bowed tile) is untraced
findings.where: draft/07-detailed-description.md ¶35 (paragraph beginning "Because the perimeter member 24 is rigid...")
findings.detail: The candidate explains why the clearance exists by asserting facts about the covering element's surface condition and flatness. No affirmative USER passage says the exposed face carries dust, grains of bonding material or surface texture, or that the covering element may be bowed. The disclosure states only that the perimeter is not intended to form a complete airtight seal, that it restricts airflow, and that air enters beneath it; it gives no cause for the ingress. This is invented engineering rationale, not inventor support.
findings.evidence: Candidate: "Because the perimeter member 24 is rigid and the exposed face 38 is neither perfectly flat nor perfectly clean, in that it carries dust, grains of bonding material 40 and its own surface texture, and the covering element 36 itself may be slightly bowed, a clearance 34 remains between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38 along at least part of the perimeter member 24". Nearest source (disclosure ¶13, repeated at conversation.md line 15): "Unlike conventional vacuum grippers or suction cups, the rigid perimeter is not intended to form a complete airtight seal and does not rely on flexible rubber or foam. Instead, it restricts airflow into the chamber while maintaining rigid contact with the tile. The air-extraction mechanism continuously removes air entering beneath the rigid perimeter". No affirmative passage anywhere describes the surface condition or flatness of the tile.
findings.fix: Replace the opening clause of ¶35 with: "Because the perimeter member 24 is not intended to form a complete airtight seal, a clearance 34 remains between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38 along at least part of the perimeter member 24, as shown enlarged in FIG. 4, ..." and delete the following sentence "The clearance 34 is far too small to be drawn to scale, and so are the departures from flatness of the exposed face 38 that give rise to it.", substituting "The clearance 34 is far too small to be drawn to scale."

findings.title: "Long, narrow, high-resistance path around the whole loop" flow-restriction mechanism is untraced
findings.detail: The candidate specifies the mechanism by which the perimeter restricts inflow — a long, narrow, high-resistance path extending around the whole loop. The disclosure says only that the perimeter "restricts airflow into the chamber"; it never describes the flow path's length, width, resistance, or that the restriction acts around the entire loop. This is an added structural/functional characterization with no affirmative source.
findings.evidence: Candidate: "the perimeter member 24 restricts the flow of ambient air into the chamber 22, and does so by presenting a long, narrow, high-resistance path around the whole loop, without closing that path." Nearest source (disclosure ¶13): "Instead, it restricts airflow into the chamber while maintaining rigid contact with the tile." No affirmative passage describes the geometry or resistance of the leakage path.
findings.fix: Replace with: "the perimeter member 24 restricts the flow of ambient air into the chamber 22 without closing that path."

findings.title: Cure behaviour attributed to the bonding material is untraced
findings.detail: The candidate ascribes a material property to the bonding material — plastic at lay-up and hardening afterwards. The disclosure names thinset, mortar, adhesive or similar bonding material but says nothing about its rheology or setting behaviour. No affirmative USER passage supports this property.
findings.evidence: Candidate: "The bonding material 40 may be thinset, mortar, tile adhesive or any similar bonding material that is plastic when the covering element 36 is laid and hardens afterwards." Nearest source (disclosure ¶5): "a vibration device for setting tiles and other covering materials into thinset, mortar, adhesive, or similar bonding material." Nothing in the disclosure addresses hardening or plasticity.
findings.fix: Amend to: "The bonding material 40 may be thinset, mortar, tile adhesive or any similar bonding material."

findings.title: "Modest in-plane resistance", "no air cushion", and delivery "at full amplitude" are untraced
findings.detail: Three untraced assertions appear in the sliding paragraph: a quantified sliding resistance, a comparison to raising an air cushion under the device, and an absolute result that vibration is delivered at full amplitude at successive positions. The disclosure says the low-friction perimeter lets the device slide freely while the vacuum maintains contact, and criticises prior art in which intensity decreases away from a fixed attachment point. It never characterises the magnitude of sliding resistance, never mentions an air cushion or air bearing, and never asserts that amplitude is undiminished across the work.
findings.evidence: Candidate: "slides under the holding force with a modest in-plane resistance"; "No mode has to be switched, no air cushion has to be raised under the device, and no grip has to be released and re-established."; "Vibration can therefore be delivered to successive areas of the covering element 36 at full amplitude, instead of falling away with distance from a single fixed attachment point." Nearest source (disclosure ¶15 and ¶7): "the low-friction perimeter allows the device to slide freely across different areas of the tile while the vacuum continuously maintains contact"; "causing vibration intensity to decrease at areas farther from the attachment point." No affirmative passage mentions an air cushion, resistance magnitude, or full amplitude.
findings.fix: Amend ¶45 to read: "The bearing face 26, being of a low-friction material, is slidable over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is maintained, and the air-extraction mechanism 20 continues to run and continues to hold the vibration device 10 down throughout the movement. No grip has to be released and re-established. Vibration can therefore be delivered to successive areas of the covering element 36, instead of the vibration intensity falling away with distance from a single fixed attachment point."

findings.title: Operator-to-operator consistency of vibration transfer is an untraced result
findings.detail: The candidate asserts a result — that transfer is consistent from one operator to the next. The disclosure asserts consistent coupling and vibration transfer supplied by the vacuum, but says nothing about variation between different operators. The inter-operator claim is an added result with no affirmative source.
findings.evidence: Candidate: "Contact is maintained by a force that does not vary with what the operator is doing, which is what makes the transfer consistent across the working area and from one operator to the next." Nearest source (disclosure ¶17): "the operator controls position using minimal pulling force while the vacuum maintains consistent coupling and vibration transfer." No passage compares operators.
findings.fix: End the sentence at "...which is what makes the transfer consistent across the working area." (delete "and from one operator to the next").

findings.title: Parallel-leakage / series-compliance model and air-film energy storage are untraced
findings.detail: The candidate advances an engineering model of the interface — the trapped film both storing and dissipating energy, and the clearance being a leakage path "in parallel" with the contact rather than a compliant layer "in series" with it. The disclosure states only that a thin layer of air may dampen vibration transfer and that rigid components transmit vibration with substantially less damping. The storage/dissipation mechanism and the parallel/series characterisation have no affirmative source.
findings.evidence: Candidate: "the film, being compressible, both stores and dissipates part of what crosses it"; "The clearance 34 is a leakage path in parallel with the contact rather than a compliant layer in series with it". Nearest source (disclosure ¶7 and ¶15): "a thin layer of air between the base and the tile may dampen vibration transfer"; "vibration energy is transferred with substantially less damping than through a flexible suction cup."
findings.fix: Replace the two clauses with disclosure-grounded wording: "...must cross the film, and the film may dampen the vibration crossing it." and "The clearance 34 admits air into the chamber 22 alongside the contact rather than lying between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38: air passes along it, edgewise, into the chamber 22, and the vibration passes across the contact beside it."

findings.title: Claim 10 limitation "incapable of transmitting compression" has no affirmative source
findings.detail: The system claim recites a negative capability limitation of the pulling element, and the description elaborates it into an absolute statement about what the operator can and cannot do. The disclosure affirmatively states only that the flexible element is pulled to move the device and that the holding force is supplied independently by the pressure differential. It never states that the element cannot transmit compression, nor that it cannot press the device down. This is a drafted inference, not inventor support, and it is currently the distinguishing structural limitation of independent claim 10.
findings.evidence: Candidate claim 10: "a flexible pulling element connected to the vibration device, the flexible pulling element being incapable of transmitting compression to the vibration device and being arranged to move the vibration device across the exposed face when tension is applied to it". Candidate ¶65: "The flexible pulling element 46 can transmit force only along its own length and, being flexible, cannot transmit compression at all. It therefore cannot press the vibration device 10 down against the covering element 36, whatever the operator does with it." Nearest source (disclosure ¶17): "In another embodiment, a rope, wire, cable, or similar flexible pulling element is connected to the device. Pulling the flexible element moves the device across the tile, while the pressure differential independently supplies the force holding the device against the surface."
findings.fix: In claim 10 replace the clause with: "a flexible pulling element connected to the vibration device, the flexible pulling element being arranged to move the vibration device across the exposed face when tension is applied to it". In ¶65 replace the first three sentences with: "The flexible pulling element 46 moves the vibration device 10 across the exposed face 38 when the operator applies tension to it. The force holding the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 is supplied independently, and continuously, by the pressure differential across the base 12." (retaining the remainder of the paragraph unchanged).

findings.title: FIG. 2 and FIG. 3 affirmatively negate any passage through the base, contradicting the claimed fluid communication
findings.where: figures/FIG-2-VERTICAL-SECTION-THROUGH-THE-CHAMBER.md line 9; figures/FIG-3-BOTTOM-PLAN-VIEW-OF-THE-VIBRATION-DEVICE.md line 7; against draft/08-claims.md claims 1, 10, 14 and draft/07-detailed-description.md ¶7, ¶13
findings.detail: Both briefs instruct that the base carries no opening of any kind, on the section view and on the second-side plan. The claims and description require the air-extraction mechanism, mounted on the first side, to be in fluid communication with the chamber on the second side. As specified, the drawings depict a device in which that limitation cannot be met, and no figure depicts the communication at all. The corrective USER turn removed "a through-base extraction opening, duct" as unsupported, so the repair must be silence about the route, not an added duct.
findings.evidence: FIG. 2 brief: "The slab is of even thickness, is drawn deep, and is hatched throughout, with no opening, channel or gap anywhere within it." FIG. 3 brief: "No circle, hole or other shape appears within the innermost rectangle, whose whole interior is plain white paper." Claim 1: "an air-extraction mechanism coupled to the first side and in fluid communication with the chamber". Description ¶13: "The second side 16 of the base 12 forms the upper boundary of the chamber 22, and the chamber 22 is in fluid communication with the air-extraction mechanism 20."
findings.fix: In the FIG. 2 brief delete ", with no opening, channel or gap anywhere within it" and add: "The route by which the air-extraction mechanism communicates with the chamber is not depicted in this view." In the FIG. 3 brief replace "No circle, hole or other shape appears within the innermost rectangle, whose whole interior is plain white paper." with "The interior of the innermost rectangle is plain white paper; the route by which the air-extraction mechanism communicates with the chamber is not depicted in this view." Add to draft/06-drawings.md, at the end of the FIG. 2 sentence: ", the communication between the air-extraction mechanism and the chamber not being shown."

findings.title: Figures place the perimeter loop inboard while claim 2 and the description place it at the perimeter of the second side
findings.where: figures/FIG-3-BOTTOM-PLAN-VIEW-OF-THE-VIBRATION-DEVICE.md lines 7-18; figures/FIG-2-VERTICAL-SECTION-THROUGH-THE-CHAMBER.md line 15; against draft/08-claims.md claim 2 and draft/07-detailed-description.md ¶29
findings.detail: FIG. 3 is specified as three nested rectangles in which a margin of the second side lies outside the loop, and FIG. 2 places each leg "a little inboard of the end of the slab". Claim 2 and the description of that very figure state the loop runs around the second side at its perimeter. The description also contradicts itself inside one paragraph, saying "near its perimeter" and then "at its perimeter". The disclosure is the authority and puts the loop at the perimeter, so the drawings must conform.
findings.evidence: FIG. 3 brief: "a large outermost rectangle, a middle rectangle standing just inside it, and an innermost rectangle standing far inside the middle rectangle"; "It shows both inside the loop, as the field within the innermost rectangle, and outside the loop, as the margin between the outermost and middle rectangles." FIG. 2 brief: "each standing a little inboard of the end of the slab". Claim 2: "wherein the perimeter member is a closed loop that runs around the chamber at a perimeter of the second side." Description ¶29: "a rigid loop, or skirt, that runs round the second side 16 near its perimeter. In the embodiment of FIG. 3 the perimeter member 24 is a closed loop running around the second side 16 at its perimeter." Source (disclosure ¶11): "The perimeter of the second side is formed as a rigid loop or skirt made from a low-friction material".
findings.fix: In the FIG. 3 brief reduce the geometry to two nested rectangles: the outermost rectangle is the outer edge of the loop, coincident with the outline of the second side, and the innermost rectangle is the inner edge of the loop; identify 24 deep inside the band between them and 16 well inside the broad plain field within the innermost rectangle; delete the sentence about the margin outside the loop and the reference to a "middle rectangle" throughout. In the FIG. 2 brief replace "each standing a little inboard of the end of the slab" with "each standing at an end of the slab". In description ¶29 replace "near its perimeter" with "at its perimeter".

findings.title: FIG. 1 shows the device standing directly on the tile with the perimeter member omitted
findings.where: figures/FIG-1-PERSPECTIVE-VIEW-OF-THE-VIBRATION-DEVICE-IN-USE.md lines 7-10; against draft/07-detailed-description.md ¶7, ¶29 and draft/06-drawings.md line 1
findings.detail: The brief renders the base as a slab whose front side face is a broad band with plain tile directly below it and nothing between. The description requires the perimeter member to stand proud of the second side, terminate in the bearing face, and be the member that contacts the exposed face, so in a perspective of the device in use the base cannot sit on the tile. As specified, FIG. 1 depicts the base itself resting on the covering element, which contradicts the claimed and described load path and leaves the only element that touches the tile invisible in the sole in-use perspective.
findings.evidence: FIG. 1 brief: "The base 12 is the flat slab every other body stands on ... It is drawn thick, so its near front side face is a broad unbroken band along the whole front of the machine, with plain tile below it and no body in front of it." Description ¶29: "A perimeter member 24 stands proud of the second side 16 and surrounds the chamber 22"; ¶7: "The perimeter member 24 extends from the second side 16 around the chamber 22 and terminates in a bearing face 26 that contacts the exposed face 38."
findings.fix: In the FIG. 1 brief, add a body: "- The perimeter member 24 is a shallow rectangular band standing under the slab and running round its underside at its edge, so the slab is held clear of the tile by that band; its outward-facing front and left surfaces are visible below the slab, and it is the only body touching the tile. Identified well inside its visible front surface." Amend the front-face sentence to "...with the perimeter member below it and plain tile below that". Add 24 to both numeral lists for FIG. 1 (giving 10, 12, 18, 20, 24, 44, still within the eight-numeral cap).

findings.title: Numeral 36 means a single covering element in FIG. 2 and FIG. 4 but a multi-tile floor in FIG. 5, and is labelled on a tile the device does not rest on
findings.where: figures/FIG-5-SECOND-EMBODIMENT-WITH-A-PULLING-ELEMENT.md line 7; against draft/numerals.md line 15, draft/07-detailed-description.md ¶5 and figures/FIG-2 line 17, figures/FIG-4 line 14
findings.detail: The numeral table defines 36 as "covering element" (singular), the description defines it as the single element laid on the bonding material and vibrated, and FIG. 2 and FIG. 4 label 36 on the one band beneath the device. FIG. 5 assigns 36 to a floor of several tiles and then places the label on a bare tile at the lower right that the device is expressly not standing on. One numeral therefore denotes two different things, and in FIG. 5 it points away from the element being treated.
findings.evidence: FIG. 5 brief: "The covering element 36 is a flat floor of a few large square tiles in perspective... The tile at the lower right of the sheet is drawn large and is left entirely bare: nothing stands on it... Identified well inside that bare tile surface at the lower right"; and, of the device, "standing on a tile farther back in the view, above the bare tile at the lower right and not on it". Compare draft/numerals.md: "| 36 | covering element |"; FIG. 4 brief: "The covering element 36 is the upper band."; description ¶5: "A covering element 36, which may be a tile or other covering material, has been laid onto a bed of bonding material 40".
findings.fix: In the FIG. 5 brief, describe the floor as "a flat floor of a few large square tiles in perspective" without a numeral, and re-anchor 36 to the element being treated: "- The covering element 36 is the tile on which the vibration device stands. Identified well inside the broad exposed surface of that tile, clear of the joint lines that bound it and clear of every body standing on it." Adjust the device sentence so the device stands on a large tile with an ample bare area of its own surface visible around the assembly.

findings.title: Component layout and inter-body spacing in FIG. 1 and FIG. 5 are untraced
findings.detail: Both briefs fix an arrangement of the first-side components — motor at the left end, extraction mechanism to its right, handle at the right end, all three separate and touching nowhere. The disclosure states only that the vibration motor is coupled to the first side, that the air-extraction mechanism is also coupled to the first side, and that the device may include one or more handles. No affirmative passage assigns positions along the base, an order of the bodies, or a non-contact relationship between them; the non-contact relationship in particular is a stated structural relationship, not a neutral rendering choice.
findings.evidence: FIG. 1 brief: "Three separate bodies stand on the top face of the slab, spaced apart along it and touching one another nowhere."; "a rectangular housing standing on the top face of the slab at its left end"; "standing on the top face of the slab to the right of the motor housing, touching that housing nowhere"; "a grip standing on the top face of the slab at its right end". FIG. 5 brief: "a rectangular motor housing at its left end, a rectangular pump housing standing on the slab to the right of that housing, and a small upright block standing on the slab at its right end, the three bodies touching one another nowhere." Nearest source (disclosure ¶11 and ¶17): "providing a vibration motor coupled to a first side of a rigid base. An air-extraction mechanism, such as a vacuum pump, is also coupled to the first side"; "The device may include one or more handles".
findings.fix: In both briefs, delete every assertion that the bodies touch one another nowhere and state only what the source supports plus the separation needed for legible leaders: "Three bodies stand on the top face of the slab and are spaced apart along it so that each presents a clear surface for its own numeral." Retain the left/right placements solely as drawing positions by rewording to "one body toward one end of the slab", "a second body along the slab beside it", "a third body toward the other end", without asserting any functional ordering.

findings.title: Attachment of the pulling element at the left end of the slab, and the unlabelled handle in the second embodiment, are untraced
findings.detail: The brief fixes where the flexible pulling element joins the device (the left end of the slab, i.e. to the base at a specified end) and also depicts a handle body in the pulling embodiment without a numeral. The disclosure says only that the flexible element "is connected to the device" and never states the point of attachment; the corrective USER turn lists "pulling-element attachment" formations among features already found unsupported. An unnumbered handle in the second embodiment also leaves depicted structure unidentified.
findings.evidence: FIG. 5 brief: "The path runs from the left end of the slab away to the left, sags gently, and passes off the left edge of the sheet in one unbroken sweep"; "a small upright block standing on the slab at its right end". Nearest source (disclosure ¶17): "In another embodiment, a rope, wire, cable, or similar flexible pulling element is connected to the device. Pulling the flexible element moves the device across the tile". No passage locates the connection.
findings.fix: Reword to "The path meets the vibration device at the slab and runs away from it over the floor, sagging gently, and passes off the edge of the sheet in one unbroken sweep", deleting the end-specific attachment. Either label the upright block "handle 44" and add 44 to both numeral lists for FIG. 5 (giving 10, 36, 44, 46), or delete the block from FIG. 5 so no unidentified body is depicted.

findings.title: Handle recited as coupled to the base is an untraced connection
findings.detail: The description and FIG. 1 fix the handle's attachment to the base. The disclosure states only that the device may include one or more handles used primarily for guiding; it does not say what the handle is coupled to. The guiding-not-pressing function is fully supported; the attachment point is not.
findings.evidence: Candidate ¶59: "One or more handles 44 may be coupled to the base 12." Nearest source (disclosure ¶17): "The device may include one or more handles used primarily for guiding the machine rather than pressing it against the surface."
findings.fix: Amend ¶59 to: "The vibration device 10 may include one or more handles 44." and leave the remainder of the paragraph, which is supported, unchanged. In the FIG. 1 brief, describe the handle as "a grip carried on the machine, standing clear of the other bodies".

findings.title: "Carries vibration across itself without loss" contradicts the qualified damping statements elsewhere
findings.detail: The joint between the perimeter member and the base is said to carry vibration "without loss", an absolute. Every other statement in the application, and the disclosure itself, is qualified: "substantially undiminished", "substantially less damping". The absolute is both internally inconsistent and unsupported.
findings.evidence: Candidate ¶29: "The joint between the perimeter member 24 and the base 12 is rigid and carries vibration across itself without loss." Compare ¶11: "it transmits that energy to the perimeter member 24 substantially undiminished"; ¶49: "with substantially less damping". Source (disclosure ¶15): "vibration energy is transferred with substantially less damping than through a flexible suction cup."
findings.fix: Amend to: "The joint between the perimeter member 24 and the base 12 is rigid and carries vibration across itself substantially undiminished."

findings.title: FIG. 5 brief calls numeral 46 a "cord", a term used nowhere else in the application
findings.detail: The numeral table, claims and description consistently use "flexible pulling element" (rope, wire or cable). The FIG. 5 brief introduces "cord", a fourth term that appears in no filing section and narrows the disclosed alternatives. Numeral 46 must carry one name across the text, the table and the briefs.
findings.evidence: FIG. 5 brief: "The flexible pulling element 46 is the one slack cord on the sheet". Compare draft/numerals.md: "| 46 | flexible pulling element |"; claim 11: "wherein the flexible pulling element is a rope, a wire or a cable."
findings.fix: Replace "the one slack cord on the sheet" with "the one slack flexible line on the sheet", and use "flexible pulling element" or "the line" for every later reference in the brief.

findings.title: FIG. 2 brief and the FIG. 2 text references disagree on what the sheet shows
findings.detail: The brief omits the motor and the air-extraction mechanism from FIG. 2 and does not label the vibration device 10, yet the description says FIG. 1 and FIG. 2 show the vibration device 10 in use, and the Brief Description calls FIG. 2 a side elevation of the vibration device of FIG. 1 without stating that the first-side equipment is omitted. The brief also depicts and labels the covering element 36, which the Brief Description does not mention for FIG. 2.
findings.evidence: FIG. 2 brief: "The equipment on top of the plate is omitted" and "The covering element 36 is the hatched band across the bottom". draft/06-drawings.md: "FIG. 2 is a side elevation of the vibration device of FIG. 1, taken in vertical section through the base, the chamber and the perimeter member." Description ¶5: "FIG. 1 and FIG. 2 show a vibration device 10 in use".
findings.fix: Amend draft/06-drawings.md line 3 to: "FIG. 2 is a vertical sectional view of the vibration device of FIG. 1 resting on a covering element, taken through the base, the chamber and the perimeter member, the vibration motor and the air-extraction mechanism being omitted for clarity." Amend description ¶5 to: "FIG. 1 shows a vibration device 10 in use, FIG. 2 shows it in vertical section, and FIG. 4 shows the bedded layers beneath it in enlarged detail."
